commit.message:
itest+lntest: cover the BOLT-02 feerate and reserve rejections

In this commit, we add the integration coverage that the daemon-side
behavior change calls for, exercising both BOLT-02 rejections end to end
over the normal funding flow, in both directions: a feerate the fundee
considers unreasonable and one it accepts, and an initial commitment whose
outputs both sit at or below the reserve the initiator named, and the same
channel shape at a feerate where they don't.

The fundee's bound is derived from its own estimate, so driving the check
takes two nodes that disagree about the current feerate. We give each node
its own --fee.url pointing at a fee service the test controls, relying on
extra args being appended after the harness's own --fee.url, where the last
occurrence of a scalar option wins.

Reaching the reserve case takes more than a large reserve: the fundee caps
the reserve it will accept at a fifth of the channel capacity, and the
initiator's balance has to fall below that cap while staying above the
two-times-dust guard in NewChannelReservation, or an earlier check is what
would reject the channel. A small tweakless channel carrying a commitment
fee worth most of its capacity is what lands in that band, so the rate is
derived from the commitment weight rather than hardcoded, and the premises
are asserted rather than assumed.

funding: bound the commit fee rate an initiator can impose on us

In this commit, we add the other half of the BOLT-02 requirement here: the
receiver MUST fail the channel if it considers feerate_per_kw unreasonably
large. The spec leaves the threshold up to us, so we take the same approach
as CLN and Eclair and cap at 10x our own estimate for the same conf target
(3) we'd use for a channel we open ourselves.

A pure multiple of our estimate is a bit brittle on its own: on a quiet
chain, or when the estimator falls back to the relay fee, 10x of a very
small number is still a very small number, and we'd start turning away
channels opened at a rate that's perfectly sane in absolute terms. So we
floor the bound at 100 sat/vbyte, which no realistic mempool needs a
commitment to beat. If the estimator errors out entirely we fall back to
that floor rather than failing the flow.

That conf target is now a single constant shared with the rate we pay on a
channel we open ourselves, so the two cannot drift apart: the point of the
bound is to track the rate we'd consider necessary for a timely unilateral
close, and a second hardcoded 3 would let those diverge silently.

The bound is consulted only after the cheap admission checks have passed,
so a peer that is over its pending-channel limit cannot drive fee
estimation work on the funding goroutine.

Since all channels are single funder today, an initiator that proposes an
absurd rate mostly burns its own capacity. But it doesn't only do that: the
open still costs us a pending channel slot, and left unchecked it lands us
with a confirmed channel that can never be used and has to be closed on
chain. Rejecting up front is cheaper for both of us.

The error carries a sentinel the funding manager can match on, so the
decision does not depend on the wording of the message we send the peer.

lnwallet: reject initial commitments that leave a channel unusable

In this commit, we replace the single balance check on the initial commitment
with the two checks that decide whether such a channel could ever be used:
the BOLT-02 requirement the receiver of open_channel MUST apply, and a
comparison of each output against the reserve its own side must maintain.

The first is the spec's, and it is what the previous revision of this commit
did alone. The spec measures both to_local and to_remote against the single
channel_reserve_satoshis the initiator named in open_channel, which is the
reserve the initiator requires of us. It stays because it is a MUST, even
though it can reject a channel the initiator could still spend on: that
happens when the reserve we name in accept_channel is the lower of the two,
and the spec requires the rejection anyway. That case is pinned by a test so
a later change cannot drop it by accident.

The second is additive. It compares to_local against the reserve the
initiator named for us and to_remote against the reserve we named for them in
accept_channel, which is exactly the condition under which neither side can
add an HTLC. The two reserves are independent, so this is not the same check
as the first, and neither implies the other: it catches the channel the spec
comparison accepts where neither side can spend, for example an initiator
naming a minimal reserve of us while its own balance lands at or below the
reserve we require of it.

That second check is a local policy, in places stricter than the letter of
the spec, and is deliberately additive rather than a reinterpretation of the
first. It costs us no usable channel: every rejection it contributes beyond
the spec's is a channel where neither side can spend, which the property test
asserts directly.

Both checks run in handleSingleContribution rather than in
NewChannelReservation, as that's the first point where both reserves are
known: the one the initiator imposes on us arrives in open_channel, while the
one we impose on them is only settled once the channel acceptor (which may
override our default) has had its say.

The error carries a sentinel the funding manager can match on, so the decision
does not depend on the wording of the message we send the peer.

commit.message:
docs: add release notes for the actor non-blocking sends

In this commit, we add a release note for the non-blocking send, overflow,
AskThen, and shutdown join additions to the actor module.

actor: require lnd/queue v1.2.1

In this commit, we bump the queue requirement from v1.1.1 to v1.2.1.
backpressure_mailbox.go uses queue.BackpressureQueue, DropCheckFunc,
AsDropPredicate and NewBackpressureQueue, which v1.1.1 doesn't have. The
module only built because of the replace directive pointing at ../queue,
and replace directives are not inherited, so a module importing actor
failed with undefined: queue.BackpressureQueue unless it bumped queue
itself. The module now also builds with the replace directives removed.

actor: add Done, StopAndWait and ShutdownAndWait to join Receive

In this commit, we let an owner stop an actor and know that no Receive
is still running. Stop and ActorSystem.Shutdown only cancel the actor's
context, so a caller that closes the stores a behavior uses right after
them can race with a Receive that is mid-flight, and an abandoned or
timed-out Future proves nothing about that.

Actor.Done is closed once the processing goroutine has exited, after
the loop and the drain of undelivered messages. StopAndWait stops the
actor and blocks until Done or the caller's context expires, and
ActorSystem.ShutdownAndWait does the same for every managed actor. A nil
return is a join: the last Receive has returned and none will start. An
actor that was never started has nothing to join, so Stop closes Done
for it directly.

The join only holds for a behavior that returns when the context it is
passed is cancelled, which the doc comments state.

actor: add AskThen to receive an Ask reply as a later message

In this commit, we add AskThen, the pipe-to-self form of Ask. It sends
the request, returns immediately, and later delivers wrap(result) to the
caller's own ref as an ordinary message. A behavior handles the reply in
a later turn instead of calling Await inside Receive, which deadlocks
when the callee is, transitively, waiting on the caller.

AskThen never blocks its calling goroutine. Inside a receive turn the
request takes the in-turn send path, so a full target mailbox spills to
the overflow queue. From any other goroutine it is a TryAsk, so a full
mailbox is delivered to self as an ErrMailboxFull result.

Completion is best effort and detached, but never silently lost. The
result is retained and its delivery retried with TryTell while self is
alive and busy. It is dropped only when self has stopped, and then the
drop is logged, the message goes to the DLO, and an optional
WithDropHandler is called, so the caller can reconcile. A timeout
abandons the wait rather than the request, and the doc comment says that
a caller that needs a durable outcome must reconcile instead of relying
on the reply.

The design follows AskThen in wavelength's baselib/actor.

actor: never park sends made from inside a receive turn

In this commit, we make a send issued from an actor's own receive turn
non-blocking. Parking an actor on a full mailbox stalls its whole
mailbox, and a cycle of actors that do so deadlocks.

The actor loop now stamps the context handed to the behavior with a
turn marker, which is cleared when the turn returns. A Tell or Ask made
with such a context goes through a new in-turn path on the default
ChannelMailbox: it uses the channel when there is room and nothing is
queued ahead of it, and otherwise spills into a bounded overflow queue
that the receive loop refills the channel from, oldest first.

The queue is capped at ActorConfig.MailboxOverflowLimit, defaulting to
DefaultMailboxOverflowLimit. A send at the cap fails with
ErrMailboxOverflow, which an Ask surfaces on its Future. Tell can't
return an error, so it logs the drop. A context that outlives its turn,
in a goroutine the behavior spawned, parks like any other producer.
WithoutTurn clears the marker explicitly.

Delivery order is acceptance order. TrySend reports full while the
overflow is non-empty, and an ordinary blocking Send from outside the
actor first waits for the overflow to drain instead of writing to the
channel ahead of it. An owner can therefore enqueue a shutdown or
barrier message and know it runs after everything already accepted.
Drain yields the overflow after the channel.

The Mailbox interface is unchanged: the in-turn path is an optional
interface that ChannelMailbox implements.

This is ported from the in-turn send design in wavelength's
baselib/actor, with the Send ordering added.

actor: add non-blocking TryTell and TryAsk

In this commit, we add TryTell and TryAsk to the actor reference
interfaces. Tell and Ask park the caller when the target's mailbox is
full, which is unsafe for a plain goroutine, such as an event loop, that
must keep servicing other work.

TryTell returns ErrMailboxFull instead of waiting for room. TryAsk
returns a Future that is already completed with the failure, so the
caller learns of it without parking. Neither blocks from any goroutine,
whether or not it is an actor. A stopped actor is reported as
ErrActorTerminated, with a TryTell routed to the DLO, and a closed
mailbox as the new ErrMailboxClosed.

The mailbox's existing TrySend already provides the primitive; this
commit exposes it on the refs and the router.

The design follows the non-parking sends in wavelength's baselib/actor.

multi: add .mailmap for release note contributors

The release notes generate their contributor list from the Git author
names of the release's commits. Several contributors commit under more
than one name, e.g. a GitHub handle and their name, or a different name
for commits made through the GitHub web interface, so the same person
was listed twice or under a name the release notes never used.

Map these identities to the names already listed in earlier release
notes. Each mapping is backed by a shared email or GitHub account.
